analysis.one_liner: Blocks the government from requiring companies to disclose their greenhouse gas emissions.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 13 Republican cosponsors and no Democrats, died in the House Financial Services Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law that publicly traded companies cannot be forced to report their greenhouse gas emissions — including emissions from their supply chains and customers, known as "Scope 3" emissions — or to provide independent certifications of those emissions [S2][S3]. It was aimed squarely at the SEC's work on a climate disclosure rule for public companies. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies — most directly fossil fuel producers and other large emitters — would be shielded from any legal requirement to report their emissions or their supply chains' emissions, avoiding the cost of measuring, verifying, and certifying that data [S2][S3]. Companies could still disclose voluntarily, but investors and the public could no longer count on comparable, required reporting across the market [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large public companies and fossil fuel producers

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that under the securities laws, no issuer of stock may be construed as required to disclose its greenhouse gas emissions or consumption — or those of its supply chain and consumers, the emissions usually called Scope 3 [S3].
It also bars any requirement to provide independent certification of emissions data, so companies would avoid the cost of third-party verification of their climate numbers [S3].
By putting the ban in statute, it would take the decision away from the SEC, which had been developing a rule requiring public companies to report climate-related risks and emissions [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Investors and the public. Shareholders who use emissions data to judge climate and regulatory risk — from flood-exposed facilities to carbon costs — would lose the guarantee of standardized, required disclosures, and the public would have a harder time tracking the emissions of major companies and their supply chains [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would permanently strip investors of standardized emissions data across all public companies. A shareholder who wants to know whether a company's supply chain is exposed to carbon rules or physical climate risk would have no required source for that information, and companies that measure emissions loosely or not at all could look cleaner than they are [S3].
Because the ban would be written into statute rather than left to regulators, it could not be revisited by the SEC as climate reporting standards mature — even if investors demanded them [S3].

An honest supporter would concede that the bill went further than blocking a specific rule: it would bar any emissions disclosure requirement, including for supply-chain (Scope 3) emissions that many large companies were already beginning to report voluntarily, potentially leaving the U.S. out of step with reporting rules developing in Europe [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to companies is real but narrow: lower compliance costs from not measuring, verifying, and filing emissions data [S3]. The cost falls on investors and the public, who lose the legal guarantee of comparable climate information about the companies they own and the products they buy [S2][S3]. Since the bill was a one-sentence ban that pre-empted an ongoing regulatory process rather than a carefully designed alternative, its design favored the companies it shielded, and the bill never advanced far enough for those trade-offs to be debated on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Beth Van Duyne introduced the bill on April 1, 2022, with ten original cosponsors, all Republicans [S3].
Thirteen Republicans cosponsored the bill in total; no Democrat did [S4].
The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee the same day, and the committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the SEC kept its authority to write climate disclosure rules, and investors kept the possibility of required emissions reporting. The companies the bill would have shielded gained nothing beyond avoiding a floor fight.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The SEC's authority; the companies gained nothing

for.name: Beth Van Duyne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited ten original Republican cosponsors.

against.name: Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote, letting it die in committee.

against.name: Gary Gensler
against.what_they_did: Led the SEC's climate disclosure rulemaking that the bill was written to block; the bill's premise was that no emissions disclosure should be required.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on; with Democrats controlling the House and its Financial Services Committee, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill would exempt these companies and their supply chains from any requirement to report greenhouse gas emissions — the data used in climate rules, investor pressure, and public accountability [S2][S3]. Their interest in avoiding measurement runs against investors' and the public's interest in knowing their emissions.

Any issuer of securities would be freed from emissions reporting, including Scope 3 emissions from supply chains and customers, saving compliance costs [S3]. The saving comes at the price of transparency for the shareholders who own the companies.

industries.industry: Climate data and ESG certification firms
industries.note: The bill bars any requirement for independent certification of emissions data, cutting off a would-be mandate for third-party verification firms [S3]. Their loss mirrors the public's loss of verified emissions numbers.
